newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela denies threat to quit over economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Mandela denies threat to quit over economic policy.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Friday he was confident that his communist and labour allies broadly supported the government's macro-economic framework for growth and development.

Mandela vehemently denied a newspaper report attributed to senior sources in his ruling African National Congress (ANC) saying he threatened to quit the party leadership if critics of the market-friendly policy were not silenced.
"There was never anything of the sort...For me to threaten to resign because there has been criticism, that is something I'd never do," he told reporters in Cape Town.

The Johannesburg Star said Mandela threatened to resign as president of the ANC if South African Communist Party deputy general secretary Jeremy Cronin was not sacked for his public criticism of the government's economic policy.
Mandela confirmed that he had initiated a discussion at a recent meeting of the ANC's National Executive Committee about party discipline, but said he had named no one and had not made any threats.
"I am confident in my power to persuade people when I am right, and if I am wrong I allow my organisation to overrule me," he said.
Mandela, 78, has said he will stand down as leader of the ANC at its conference in December 1997 and will not seek the presidency in the next general election in 1999.

His ANC rules in a formal alliance with the Communist Party and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), which have both publicly criticised the macro-economic policy published by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on June 14.
The programme calls for privatisation, government spending cuts and investment incentives to push growth from under three percent a year now to six percent by the turn of the century.

"There is no doubt that Cosatu and the (Communist) Party support the broad framework of the macro-economic policy. They may want to make an amendment here and an amendment there...but that process is a healthy one and can only strengthen the alliance," Mandela said.
There are active debates within both the Communist party and COSATU at present about whether to continue the alliance with the economically moderate ANC in 1999.
Both groups are critical of the ANC's positions on fiscal discipline, market economics and the privatisation of state-owned utilities.
Some members also criticise Mandela's commitment to reconciliation with the country's former white rulers.
An ANC source said Mandela did warn at the executive committee meeting that loyalty to the ANC should outweigh loyalty to the communist party or COSATU on matters of agreed policy.
The source said Mandela told the meeting that communists and unionists unable to back the party line in public should "find another political home".
He said Mandela encouraged debate within party structures.
